lesson.text: Quick memory: who are some people who help a community? (Doctors, firefighters, refuse collectors, volunteers and more.) Many of their services are run by a council. Who runs a town, and who pays?

Towns and cities are run by a local council. Local people vote in an election to choose councillors, who speak for them. In many places a mayor leads the council. They meet to decide what the town needs.
The council looks after services that everyone shares: roads and street lights, bin collections and recycling, parks and playgrounds, libraries, and often schools.
Services cost money. People who live and work in the town pay taxes, and the council spends them on services. One family could never pay for a library, but thousands of families together can.
Worked example: a new playground costs 1,200 gold. If 60 families share the cost equally, each pays 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20 gold, and every child in town can play there.
There is never enough money for everything, so councils must choose: a new library roof, or a new bus shelter? They ask people what they think and must show how the money was spent.
Some jobs are too big for one town. A country's government makes laws for the whole country and looks after things like the army. The council looks after local things.
Try it in the world: be a town council with your friends: list what your town needs, share out 100 gold of taxes, then build the service you chose first. Next: deciding together.

choices: a council, chosen by local people
exercises.explain: A local council, with councillors chosen by local people in an election.

exercises.prompt: Which of these does a council look after?
exercises.hint: It is shared by everyone in the town.
exercises.explain: Parks are shared services that the council looks after.

exercises.prompt: Taxes help to pay for roads, parks and libraries.
exercises.hint: Where does the council's money come from?
exercises.explain: True: taxes paid by people and businesses pay for shared services.

exercises.prompt: Who often leads a town council?
exercises.hint: It is an old word for the head of a town.
exercises.explain: In many places a mayor leads the council.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a service we share, or something private?
exercises.hint: Can everyone in the town use it?
exercises.explain: Shared: the library, street lights and bin collections. Private: your garden, your toys and a family car.

exercises.prompt: A new bench costs 200 gold. 20 families share the cost equally. How much does each family pay?
exercises.hint: Share equally: divide the cost by the number of families.

exercises.explain: In an election: local people vote for the councillors they want.

exercises.prompt: One family could easily pay for a whole library on its own.
exercises.hint: How much does a library cost to build and run?
exercises.explain: False: a library costs far too much for one family, but thousands of families sharing the cost can pay for it.

exercises.prompt: Match each service to what it gives us.
exercises.hint: Think about why each one matters.
exercises.explain: Street lights: safe roads at night. Bins: clean streets. Libraries: books for all. Parks: places to play.

exercises.prompt: The council has money for a new library roof or a new bus shelter, not both. What should it do?
exercises.hint: Remember opportunity cost, and asking people.
choices: ask people, compare needs, explain the choice
exercises.explain: Choosing means giving something up, so the council asks people, compares the needs and explains its choice.

exercises.prompt: Who makes laws for a whole country?
exercises.hint: Some jobs are too big for one town.
exercises.explain: The country's government makes laws for the whole country; councils look after local things.

exercises.prompt: The council has 500 gold. It spends 180 gold on roads and 120 gold on the park. How much is left?
exercises.hint: Take away one cost at a time.

exercises.prompt: Councils should show people how the tax money was spent.
exercises.explain: True: it is everyone's money, so people should be able to see how it was spent.

exercises.prompt: Why do people pay taxes instead of each buying their own road?
exercises.hint: Think of the playground paid for by 60 families.
choices: sharing costs pays for things all can use
exercises.explain: Sharing costs lets a community pay for roads, parks and libraries that everyone can use.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: looked after by the town council, or by the country's government?
exercises.hint: Is it for one town, or for the whole country?
exercises.explain: The council looks after local things: street lights, bins and the park. The country's government looks after the army and makes laws for everyone.
